summary: IMAP's OBJECTID capability (RFC 8474) gives each mailbox a unique identifier that stays the same when the mailbox is renamed. This document extends the Sieve email filtering language (RFC 5228) so that same identifier can be used as the target of fileinto rules and to test whether a mailbox exists. Filters then keep working after folders are renamed.

plainLanguage.summary: If you rename a folder, your mail sorting rules should not break. This document lets the rules point at a folder's permanent ID number instead of its name, so changing the name does not matter.

questions: how to make sieve rules survive mailbox rename
how to keep sieve rules after renaming a folder
subtitle: Lets Sieve mail filters file messages by a mailbox's permanent ID, so renaming a folder does not break the rules.

tldr.problem: Sieve rules name target mailboxes by name. If a folder is renamed, the rule can go out of sync, and fixing it is a multistep process that can partly fail.
tldr.mechanism: The 'mailboxid' extension adds a :mailboxid argument to fileinto and :fcc, plus a mailboxidexists test, all using the immutable MAILBOXID from IMAP's OBJECTID capability.
tldr.outcome: Rules keep targeting the same mailbox after a rename, and fall back to the named mailbox if no mailbox has that ID. It is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5228.

today: RFC 9042 is a Proposed Standard from June 2021 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 5228 by adding the mailboxid capability.

sections.title: Why Mailbox IDs
sections.content:
Sieve rules (RFC 5228) are often created in graphical interfaces where users pick the target mailbox. If that mailbox is renamed, the client may update the rule and the Sieve script to match, but this is a multistep process subject to partial failures. If another IMAP client renames the folder, the rules get out of sync.

By telling fileinto to reference the immutable MAILBOXID specified by RFC 8474, rules can keep targeting the same mailbox even after it is renamed.
sections.plainLanguage: A label can change, but the drawer's secret number never does. Rules that use the number always find the right drawer.

sections.title: Capability and the :mailboxid Argument
sections.content:
Scripts using the extension MUST explicitly require the capability mailboxid, as in require "mailboxid";.

Normally fileinto delivers to the mailbox named by its positional argument. With the optional :mailboxid argument, it first checks whether a mailbox with that MAILBOXID exists in the user's personal namespace. If one is found, it is used for delivery. If not, fileinto proceeds as it would without the argument, using the named mailbox. The tag consumes one extra token, a string holding the OBJECTID of the target mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: First look for the drawer with the secret number. If it is not there, use the drawer with the label you wrote down.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Extensions
sections.content:
Mailbox extension (RFC 5490). If both :create and :mailboxid are given and no matching mailbox is found, a new mailbox is created with the name from the positional argument. It gets a different MAILBOXID, chosen by the server, not the one in the argument.

Special-use (RFC 8579). Giving both :mailboxid and :specialuse in one fileinto is an error. Tool developers are advised to use special-use rather than MAILBOXID for rules based on a special-use purpose, such as delivery to the Junk folder.

FCC (RFC 8580). The :fcc argument can also take :mailboxid. If a mailbox with that ID exists, the generated message is filed there, otherwise into the :fcc target mailbox. Combining it with :specialuse is likewise an error.

Variables (RFC 5229). No special interaction is defined, but because an OBJECTID is a string, it can contain variable expansions.
sections.plainLanguage: This feature plays nicely with other mail-sorting features, but you cannot ask for a drawer by its number and by its special job at once.

sections.title: The mailboxidexists Test
sections.content:
The syntax is mailboxidexists <mailbox-objectids: string-list>. It is true if every string given is the MAILBOXID of a mailbox that exists in the mailstore and that lets the script's user deliver messages into it. It behaves like the mailboxexists test of RFC 5490, but on IDs rather than names.

With IMAP ACL (RFC 4314), delivery is allowed if the user has the p or i rights. Without ACL, it is allowed if the READ-WRITE response code is present when the user selects the mailbox.

A true result does not guarantee a later fileinto :mailboxid succeeds. For example, the user might be over quota. The test only checks existence and permission.
sections.plainLanguage: Before putting a note in a drawer, you can ask if the drawer with that number exists and if you are allowed to use it.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
MAILBOXIDs are always generated by the server. Implementations MUST NOT let Sieve get around this by creating a mailbox with a specified ID through :create and :mailboxid in a fileinto rule for a nonexistent mailbox. Implementers should also read the security sections of RFC 5228 and RFC 8474.

IANA added the capability mailboxid to the "Sieve Extensions" registry, with contact address the EXTRA discussion list.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the mail server hands out drawer numbers. A rule cannot make up its own number for a new drawer.

data.title: Test then file by MAILBOXID
